title: Simulation-Based Analysis of the Passenger Processing System at Vertiports
sections_pages_consulted: pp. 2-4 (process review and scenarios, Fig. 3); p. 5 (SITA check-in shares; 20 s passenger weighing); pp. 6-7 (Table 2 arrival tmin/tmax; beta arrival profile 15-60 min); pp. 8-9 (Tables 5-6 IATA LoS and time-factor adaptation); pp. 10-12 (results, bunching limitation)
method_and_system_boundary: Discrete-event simulation (AnyLogic) of departing passengers only; generic vertiport 1 FATO + 5 stands; no airside coupling; walking times not modelled
factual_paraphrase: Departure process: ticketing/check-in, weight check (passenger and carry-on), security screening, then boarding; no bag drop (all carry-on) and no border control. Classic scenario = staffed counter; progressive = counter 34%, kiosk 18%, online 48% (SITA 2020). Arrival before STD compressed to 15-60 min. LoS judged by share of passengers above the IATA 'Optimum' maximum wait (NALoS), using first-class/fast-track guidelines (counter 180 s, self-service 120 s, security 180 s; weight check set to 180 s by the author). Check-in counter was the bottleneck.
decision_supported: mandatory step; service distribution/range; evaluation metric
limitation: Processing times taken from an airport-terminal dissertation (Metzner 2020) and not reported in the paper except 20 s weighing; LoS thresholds are an author adaptation of IATA ADRM, not a vertiport standard; passenger bunching and walking ignored

title: Determining infrastructure requirements for an air taxi service at Cologne Bonn Airport

factual_paraphrase: Access control to keep non-authorised persons off the manoeuvring area: U(5,20) s. Baggage check: U(30,60) s. Stand time defined as time after landing to load batteries before take-off; battery loading assumed 30 min (expert interviews + Volocopter 2X data), limiting each stand to 2 aircraft/h. FATO blocked 6 min per landing/take-off cycle. All passengers on one eVTOL share one destination; max 4 seats.

authors_or_institution: Northeast UAS Airspace Integration Research Alliance (NUAIR) et al., for NASA
title: High-Density Automated Vertiport Concept of Operations
sections_pages_consulted: Sec. 2.3.9 p. 32 (security screening); Sec. 4.6.9 p. 60 (servicing at pad, gate or parking); vertistop/vertiport/vertihub definitions p. 41; Sec. 5.1.1.1 pp. 61-63 (pre-flight); Sec. 5.1.1.2 pp. 64-65 (taxi and departure slot); Sec. 5.1.1.5 pp. 69-70 (land, taxi, deplane); Sec. 5.1.1.6.1 p. 71 (maintenance on arrival); Sec. 5.1.1.6.4 p. 73 (charging request on arrival)
method_and_system_boundary: Concept of operations by subject-matter experts; nominal and off-nominal step-by-step scenarios; no quantitative calibration
factual_paraphrase: Flight plan declares requested services and stay duration; VAS reserves resources before approval. Passengers are ticketed, screened and queued; boarding safety briefing in the boarding area. Crew confirms aircraft ready for boarding, then gate opens and status changes to boarding. Dispatch only after system check and operator authorisation; PSU re-validates departure slot before clearance. On arrival, passengers deplane and are guided away before the crew declares the aircraft deplaned and servicing starts. Charging is requested in the flight plan, reserved with its duration, and performed in situ at gate/parking or after repositioning. With minor maintenance, enplaning passengers are held in the terminal; without a substitute aircraft the flight is cancelled.
decision_supported: readiness condition; synchronization rule; charging policy
limitation: Prescriptive ConOps for automated high-density operations, not a regulation or observation; no durations, no rule for late passengers or empty seats

title: FAA Vertiport Electrical Infrastructure Study
sections_pages_consulted: p. vi (OEM survey summary); p. 1 (vertiport vs vertistop); pp. 12-13 (OEM charging data: 300-1000 kW DC, 130->300 kWh); pp. 19-20 (EVSE placement depends on ConOps, schedule and demand; chargers in TLOF footprint possible); p. 25 (passenger arrival 1-2 h before airline flight in ACY case); p. 53 (no flight scheduled until aircraft has charge to reach destination); pp. 55-56 (FCFS charging at constant power to 100%); p. 110 (conclusions)
method_and_system_boundary: Site assessment and agent-based flight/charging scheduling model for seven NY/NJ sites; OEM survey of six manufacturers
factual_paraphrase: OEMs gave incomplete data; peak DC charging 300 kW-1 MW and battery 130 to >300 kWh. A flight is not scheduled until the aircraft holds enough charge for the destination. Charging was FCFS at constant power until 100% SOC; NREL notes a constant-to-80% then linear taper as the simplest realistic curve but did not calibrate it. Vertistops are minimally developed touch-and-go sites where charging is unlikely to be justified. EVSE placement must follow the site ConOps, flight schedule and demand.
limitation: Site-specific; OEM identities anonymised; charging curve not certified; 'vertistop unlikely to charge' cites Schweiger and Preis 2022 rather than a rule

title: Urban Air Mobility Systematic Review of Scientific Publications and Regulations for Vertiport Design and Operations
sections_pages_consulted: pp. 4-5 (vertiport/vertistop definitions from FAA EB 105 industry draft, ASTM WK59317 and Uber Elevate); p. 31 (short vs long turnaround times and charging)
method_and_system_boundary: Systematic review of literature and regulation
factual_paraphrase: FAA EB 105 industry draft defined a vertistop as a site like a vertiport where no charging, fuelling, maintenance or storage is permitted; ASTM WK59317 defines a vertistop as a minimally developed facility for boarding and discharging, comparable to a bus stop. Short turnaround (0.5-10 min) reflects touch-and-go vertistops where only boarding/deboarding occurs and full charging is unlikely; long turnaround (30 min or more) reflects equipped vertiports.
limitation: The no-charging definition comes from a draft later superseded; turnaround ranges are compiled assumptions from other studies

method_and_system_boundary: Official design guidance supplementing AC 150/5390-2D; geometry and safety
factual_paraphrase: For design, vertistops and vertipads are the same as vertiports regarding fundamental design requirements. Parking clearances may need to grow for charging equipment and passenger boarding ramps; passenger walkways must minimise exposure during loading/unloading. No consensus on charging classes or connectors; operators may use fixed, mobile, battery storage or swapping solutions.
limitation: Design guidance only; no operational rule on when charging occurs or on passenger presence during charging
